items.title: The Artificial Life of Politics: Synthetic Avatars and the Manufacture of Political Presence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence allows political presence to be produced without the participation of those whose presence is displayed. Research has treated such media mainly as false records, or has studied AI presented as a political agent. This article examines a third phenomenon: AI that supplies the face, voice, or body through which human operators make a political appearance. It develops the concept of synthetic political avatars, analyzes them by referent, claimed basis of standing, accountability, and disclosure, and distinguishes four kinds of claims they make: to be a specific person, to be a typical member of a group, to speak for a group, and to present content as the work of a group. A layered comparison covers nineteen documented avatars in nine countries of the Global South between 2023 and 2026, set against contrast cases from other regions, institutional uses, and AI-driven candidacies. Across the core configurations, the cases reveal recurring gaps between synthetic presence and the strongest available basis of standing, while disclosure and authorization vary independently. Procedural governance of synthetic presence exists mainly in museums and foundations, not in electoral politics. The cases also support propositions about synthetic succession, the substitution of absent leaders, and the use of identity markers without participation. Generative AI lowers the cost of producing political presence without lowering the cost of authorizing or attributing it, and labeling, on its own, does not close that gap.

items.title: THE arXiv CONUNDRUM
items.abstract: The preprint repository arXiv was founded in 1991 to dismantle the gatekeeping, commercial rent-seeking, and temporal stagnation inherent in legacy peer-reviewed academic publishing. Funded generously by the late James Simons and the Simons Foundation to establish an unencumbered, public channel of scientific priority, the platform was conceived as an architectural “hack” against bureaucratic inertia. Over the past decade, however, arXiv has undergone institutional ossification, reconstructing the very medieval gatehouse it was chartered to overthrow.This treatise analyzes the structural pathology of modern preprint moderation through an epistemological and sociotechnical lens. We document a profound procedural absurdity:the demand by arXiv moderation panels that independent researchers must “first publish in a peer-reviewed legacy journal and provide proof of publication” before being permitted to deposit a preprint. We expose the inherent circularity of converting an unrefereed preprint exchange into a lagging post-publication repository. Furthermore, we examine the systemic hubris of anonymous moderation tiers overruling established pioneers of theoretical physics—including the documented reprimand of Alexander (Sasha) Migdal for endorsing foundational hydrodynamic research. Grounded in Robert K. Merton’s sociology of science, Thomas Kuhn’s paradigm dynamics, and the economics of open-access networks, we demonstrate how algorithmic and opaque editorial screening enforces intellectual monoculture, suppresses radical first-principles inquiry, and betrays the egalitarian vision of Jim Simons and Paul Ginsparg.

items.title: The Digital Product Passport: Challenges for SMEs and the Role of AI-Powered Compliance Solutions
items.abstract: The introduction of the Digital Product Passport (DPP) is changing the requirements for the collection, management, and long-term availability of product information within the European Union. Companies increasingly need to address structured data, interoperable formats, and traceability throughout their supply chains. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), in particular, face the challenge of meeting regulatory requirements without having to initiate extensive IT projects. This article examines key criteria for evaluating software solutions designed to support the implementation of Digital Product Passports. Particular attention is given to the automated processing of existing product documentation, supplier data integration, technical interoperability, and the long-term availability of digital product information. Using DPP-Flash as an example, the article explores how an AI-powered approach focused on simplifying workflows may address these challenges. The analysis also highlights why the practical suitability of a software solution cannot be assessed solely by its range of features. Data quality, the actual implementation of applicable regulatory requirements, and operational reliability are equally important. The findings suggest that accessible, AI-assisted solutions may offer a promising approach for companies seeking to establish DPP processes without unnecessarily increasing administrative complexity. 1. Introduction Regulatory changes often become a concrete operational concern for companies only when they begin to affect established processes. With the Digital Product Passport, however, it is already becoming apparent that the issue goes beyond adding another information page or placing a QR code on product packaging. It represents a broader change in how product-related information is collected, organized, and made accessible. Through Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, commonly known as the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), the European Union has established a framework that provides for the gradual introduction of Digital Product Passports for specified product groups. The exact information requirements and implementation dates depend on the relevant product-specific legislation. For certain batteries, the EU Battery Regulation already provides for a battery passport requirement from 18 February 2027. This creates a challenge that may initially appear technical but actually affects several business functions. Product management, procurement, quality management, IT, and compliance must work with information that has not necessarily been organized consistently. For companies managing large product portfolios and numerous suppliers, the resulting effort can be substantial. The key question is therefore not simply how a Digital Product Passport can be generated technically. It is how the entire process, from data collection to subsequent updates, can be organized in a reliable and economically viable manner. 2. The Real Challenge Lies in the Data In many companies, the information required for a Digital Product Passport already exists. The problem is that it is often distributed across different systems and formats. Technical data sheets may be stored as PDFs, material information may be maintained in spreadsheets, certificates may be managed separately, and certain details may need to be requested directly from suppliers. In some cases, multiple document versions exist without a clear indication of which one is current. This situation illustrates why implementing a Digital Product Passport cannot be reduced to creating a digital document. First, the relevant information must be identified and consolidated. It must then be checked for completeness, accuracy, currency, and correct product assignment. Depending on the product category, additional requirements may apply to data formats, identification, access rights, and registration. A system that merely makes existing documents available online therefore addresses only part of the problem. The same applies to an automated solution that extracts information quickly but does not provide sufficient opportunities to verify its accuracy. In my view, the central challenge is to stop treating the Digital Product Passport as an isolated output and instead understand it as the result of a continuous data management process. Only when this process can be integrated into existing business operations in a practical way does it create lasting value for a company. 3. Key Criteria for Selecting DPP Software Selecting a suitable software solution should not depend solely on the number of available features. Several criteria are particularly important for small and medium-sized enterprises. 3.1 Processing Existing Product Documentation A practical starting point is to reuse information that companies already possess rather than manually entering all data again. Software should therefore be capable of processing different document types and showing which information was extracted from which source. AI-powered data extraction can provide a practical advantage in this context. It can reduce manual effort and make large volumes of unstructured information easier to process. However, it cannot replace professional review. For regulatory information in particular, users need to understand which data was extracted automatically and which details still require confirmation or supplementation. 3.2 Interoperability and Standardized Data Formats A Digital Product Passport should not be understood as a closed collection of information within a single software platform. Where required by the applicable legislation, information must be structured, machine-readable, and exchangeable through appropriate interfaces. Open standards, unique product identifiers, and compatibility with relevant technical specifications are therefore important selection criteria. Depending on the application, technologies such as JSON-LD and GS1 Digital Link may be relevant. Whether a particular implementation meets the applicable requirements must nevertheless be assessed against the relevant specifications. 3.3 Supplier Integration A significant proportion of product-related information originates outside the company itself. Details about materials, components, or specific product characteristics may therefore need to be collected throughout the supply chain. Suitable DPP software should support this process. Relevant capabilities include structured information requests, traceable assignment of incoming data, and systematic identification of missing information. Without such functionality, companies risk digitizing only the information already available to them while leaving important data gaps unresolved. 3.4 Long-Term Availability and Data Maintenance Product information loses much of its value if it becomes inaccessible or can no longer be clearly associated with the relevant product. Companies should therefore consider hosting arrangements, data backup, change management, and the agreed duration of information availability when evaluating providers. The required retention and availability periods must reflect the applicable legal requirements. It would be misleading, however, to suggest that every Digital Product Passport must always be stored for the same period, regardless of product category or regulatory context. 3.5 Usability and Economic Feasibility Finally, software should not only be technically capable but also practical to use in everyday operations. Smaller companies often lack dedicated teams for complex IT integrations or regulatory data projects. A clear workflow, transparent pricing, and a manageable implementation process can therefore be just as important as the overall feature set. A solution that requires disproportionate internal resources to implement may ultimately fail to deliver its intended value. 4. DPP-Flash as an Example of an AI-Powered Approach Against this background, DPP-Flash represents an interesting example of software designed to simplify the introduction of Digital Product Passports. The platform is aimed particularly at companies seeking to use existing product data while reducing the effort involved in creating structured product passports. According to the publicly available product information, existing documents, including technical data sheets and other product-related materials, can be incorporated into the process. The software uses artificial intelligence to extract relevant information. The resulting data can then be reviewed and confirmed. Additional capabilities described by the provider include the generation of product passport QR codes and tools for making product information available and managing it. This approach addresses a genuine problem faced by many companies. When relevant information already exists across multiple documents, it makes economic sense to reuse those sources rather than begin with a complete manual re-entry of all available data. The interesting aspect is not AI alone, but how it is integrated into a workflow designed to minimize unnecessary steps. In everyday business operations, technology creates lasting value only when it genuinely simplifies the process while maintaining sufficient opportunities for verification and control. DPP-Flash also describes functionality for processing structured data and incorporating supplier information. The platform therefore aims to address more than the creation of an individual product passport. It also targets upstream activities involved in collecting and consolidating the necessary information. From this perspective, DPP-Flash appears particularly relevant to companies seeking a practical solution without immediately committing to a large-scale digital transformation project. items.title: The DYNABIC Approach and Architecture
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the DYNABIC framework, a comprehensive and adaptive cybersecurity solution designed to enhance the resilience of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) in the face of evolving cyber-physical threats. The framework integrates advanced technologies such as digital twins, artificial intelligence, and cyber threat intelligence to enable real-time threat detection, simulation, and response. At its core, DYNABIC employs a bidirectionally synchronized digital twin to model and simulate cyber-physical systems, supporting dynamic risk mitigation and adaptive response strategies across the four phases of the resilience cycle: Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, and Adapt. The architecture is modular and scalable, fostering collaboration among CIs and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). It includes key components such as MADT4BC, SOAR4BC, RISKM4BC, SIM4BC, AWARE4BC, and CTI4BC, which collectively support real-time monitoring, risk assessment, incident simulation, automated response, and threat intelligence sharing. The framework also incorporates a human-in-the-loop interface (AVATAR4BC) to enhance situational awareness and decision-making.

items.title: The Effect of Transformational Leadership and Employee Engagement on Employee Performance in the Service Industry
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of transformational leadership and employee engagement on employee performance within the service industry. As organizations in this sector increasingly compete on service quality, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency, understanding the human factors that drive employee performance has become a strategic priority for management. Transformational leadership, characterized by idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, is theorized to enhance employees' motivation, commitment, and willingness to exceed expected job requirements. Similarly, employee engagement, reflecting the degree of vigor, dedication, and absorption employees exhibit toward their work, is considered a critical psychological state that translates leadership influence into tangible performance outcomes. This research employs a quantitative approach using a survey method distributed to employees working in service-based organizations. Data were collected through structured questionnaires measuring transformational leadership, employee engagement, and employee performance, and were analyzed using multiple regression analysis to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings reveal that both transformational leadership and employee engagement have a positive and significant effect on employee performance, whether tested partially or simultaneously. Transformational leadership was found to strengthen employees' sense of purpose and trust in their leaders, which in turn fosters higher engagement and, consequently, improved performance outcomes. Employee engagement was also identified as a key mediating mechanism linking leadership behavior to performance results. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on leadership and human resource management by providing empirical evidence from the service industry context, where interpersonal interaction and employee behavior directly affect service delivery quality.

items.title: The Effects of Weather, Distraction, and ADHD Diagnosis on Automated-to-Manual Driving Transitions
items.abstract: As automated vehicles become more prevalent on public roadways, driver responses to critical takeover events require closer attention. This study examined how ADHD diagnosis, rain, and non-driving-related task engagement affect automated-to-manual takeover transitions. Participants completed conditionally automated drives in a simulated freeway environment that varied according to the presence of rain and distraction. Driving performance, takeover response, physiological workload, and post-drive subjective workload were assessed. Findings indicated that rain and distraction affected takeover performance, workload, speed variability, and steering variability. Results also indicated that drivers with ADHD displayed greater speed and steering variability in the presence of rain and distraction. These results suggest that reduced visibility and NDRT engagement can increase the demands of regaining manual control. Overall, the findings indicate that roadway conditions, attentional demands, and individual differences can influence takeover quality. Implications include safer in-vehicle monitoring systems, improved takeover alert systems, and targeted driver training.

items.title: THE EMERGENCE AND DEVELOPMENT OF UPBRINGING TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: This article examines the historical emergence, stages of development, and significance of upbringing technologies in contemporary pedagogical practice. It analyzes the educational and moral perspectives of Eastern thinkers from ancient times, the gradual improvement of traditional upbringing methods, and the integration of modern pedagogical technologies into educational processes. Particular attention is paid to the future prospects of upbringing technologies, including the application of digital educational tools, interactive methods, and artificial intelligence. Furthermore, the article discusses the pedagogical importance of developing moral and ethical qualities among younger generations, preserving national values, and improving contemporary approaches to upbringing. It emphasizes the need to integrate historical educational traditions with modern innovations to foster the comprehensive personal and social development of students. items.title: The evolution of entrepreneurship education in the digital era: a bibliometric roadmap of AI-driven experiential learning (2016–2026)
items.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to examine the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven experiential learning in entrepreneurship education in the digital era and to identify the main research trends, intellectual foundations and future directions shaping the field. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a bibliometric approach using 204 Web of Science-indexed articles and reviews published between 2016 and June 2026. Performance analysis and science mapping were conducted using VOSviewer 1.6.20, including publication trajectory, source performance, co-citation, document citation, author productivity, keyword co-occurrence and overlay analyses. Findings The findings show that the field has shifted from limited early activity to rapid expansion during 2024–2026, driven by growing attention to generative AI, AI literacy and educational technology. Three knowledge bases are identified: educational technology and digital pedagogy; entrepreneurship, business and management education; and sustainability-oriented transformation. Five thematic clusters further highlight behavioural competency, AI integration in higher education, socio-technical adaptation, crisis-driven experiential learning and student-centred instructional design. Originality/value The paper contributes a bibliometric research roadmap for AI-driven experiential entrepreneurship education by identifying the field's intellectual structure, thematic development and future research directions. It positions AI not only as a digital tool, but as part of a wider pedagogical shift toward adaptive, responsible and precarity-aware entrepreneurial learning ecosystems.

items.title: The Evolution of Financial Time Series Forecasting: From Classical Econometrics to Temporal Foundation Models and Multimodal LLMs
items.abstract: Financial time series forecasting sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, econometrics, and machine learning. The data generating processes involved are characterized by non-stationarity, regime-dependent volatility clustering, very low signal-to-noise ratios, and reflexive feedback between market participants and asset prices. Over roughly six decades, the dominant methodology has moved through five recognizable phases: classical linear econometrics (ARMA, ARIMA, regularized VAR, VECM), conditional volatility modeling (ARCH/GARCH families, Stochastic Volatility), recursive online signal processing (LMS, RLS, Kalman filters), deep sequence learning (LSTMs, TCNs, patch-based Transformers, State Space Models), and the contemporary period (2024–2026) of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), Temporal Language Models (TLMs), and LLMs adapted for financial reasoning. For the comparative analysis in Section 10, the deep learning phase is split into two paradigms (recurrent/convolutional networks and Transformer-based architectures), and the foundation model phase into numerical TSFMs and multimodal LLM adapters, yielding seven paradigm entries in total. This paper traces that trajectory through the lens of what we call the Capacity-Adaptability Trilemma, a three-way tension between representational capacity, online adaptability, and structural interpretability. We also review evidence on where foundation models fall short in financial contexts, including benchmark contamination and architectural mismatches that can cause large zero-shot models to underperform simple statistical baselines. To address this, we propose Econometrically-Informed Neural Networks (EINNs) as a way to embed econometric constraints into modern deep architectures. We present four self-contained synthetic experiments run on a MacBook Air M1, which offer only limited, illustrative support for these claims. First, the best model class depends on the data regime: a linear AR/ARMA baseline was best on stationary low-SNR data and across all tested SNR levels in our setup, RLS adapted best under parameter drift, and an LSTM was best only on a high-SNR nonlinear process. Second, a noise-dependent crossover exists between DLinear and PatchTST. Third, trained autoregressors and MLPs do not beat naive persistence on synthetic random walks. Fourth, a proposed VECM regularizer keeps forecast spreads stationary in a bivariate cointegrated setup, though it does so by producing spread forecasts with much lower variance than the true spread. All experiments use synthetic data, and validation on real financial series remains future work.

items.title: The Future of E-Business in the Era of the Technological Singularity
items.abstract: The accelerating development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), data-driven systems and autonomous digital platforms leads to profound transformations in modern e-business. These transformations are increasingly conceptualized through the notion of technological singularity, which is understood not as a singular future event but as an ongoing process of escalating algorithmic autonomy, systemic complexity and diminishing human controllability. The aim of the paper is to discuss the future of the development of e-business in the era of the singularity by analyzing the business model transformation, management and decision-making, cybersecurity and sustainability, and competitiveness in global markets. The main outcome of the work will be that the sustainable development of e-business in the era of the singularity requires a new balance between algorithmic autonomy and human control, between technological efficiency and social responsibility.

items.title: The Future of Social (Dis)Connection
items.abstract: Over the next decades, the nature of and possibilities for social connection will rapidly evolve with advances in artificial intelligence, mixed-reality technologies, and pervasive digital integration. Accordingly, psychological science must update how it conceptualizes and measures social connection. Here, we advance a three-part conceptual framework for understanding social (dis)connection in contemporary and future environments. First, we situate social experiences within a dynamic relational ecosystem—a system of interaction partners and channels, ambient social cues, and sociocultural contexts that together shape connection. Second, we conceptualize “alone” and “together” not as binary states but as a gradient shaped by level of physical copresence and communication (shades of aloneness and togetherness). Third, we conceptualize discrete social interactions as multidimensional, characterized by features such as interaction partner, relationship type, medium, temporality, engagement, and volition. Building on this framework, we propose five testable predictions about how social (dis)connection may evolve in the coming decades: the decoupling of objective and subjective connection, the erosion of “pure” solitude, the increasing effortfulness and value of in-person interaction, the fragmentation of shared reality, and the growing taken-for-grantedness of connection. We conclude by discussing methodological and applied implications of this framework.

items.title: The future workplace: developing the human-machine symbioscape
items.abstract: Purpose This paper develops the concept of the human-machine symbioscape to explain how work environments shape collaboration between humans and AI-enabled machines. Extending servicescape thinking from customer-employee encounters to hybrid human-machine work systems, the paper positions environmental design as a core antecedent of human–machine adaptive collaboration, with particular relevance for service and frontline settings where visibility, coordination, and role clarity are critical. Design/methodology/approach The paper is conceptual and theory building in nature. It synthesises insights from biological symbiosis, servicescape research, sociotechnical and sociomaterial theory, organisational sensemaking and team adaptation research to develop a deductive typology of the human-machine symbioscape as a three-tiered environmental construct, its cue categories, and its design-critical properties. The framework is further illustrated through a structured coding of relevant human-machine collaboration studies. Findings The paper conceptualises the symbioscape as a three-tier environmental architecture comprising physical–digital, socio-relational, and institutional–ecosystem conditions. Across these tiers, six cue categories shape what human and AI-enabled actors can notice, how they coordinate work, and how collaborative routines are reinforced over time. Drawing on Weick's sensemaking theory, the framework links these tiers to enactment, selection, and retention processes, and explains how they influence adaptation speed, adaptation effectiveness, and adaptation persistence in human–AI collaboration. Research limitations/implications The paper is purely conceptual and does not empirically test the proposed relationships. Its evidence base is limited to published studies and illustrative coding, with a strong emphasis on service and frontline contexts. It identifies an agenda for future research around operationalising symbioscape constructs, testing the proposed relationships empirically, and examining how individual tiers and cross-tier configurations jointly affect human–machine work. Practical implications The symbioscape framework provides managers with a structured lens for designing AI-enabled workplaces. It highlights how deliberate choices in physical–digital visibility and interface design, socio-relational workflow sequencing and interaction load, and institutional governance, training, and role architecture can improve the speed, quality and durability of human–machine adaptation. The framework can be used to diagnose service work environments, where frontline employees must coordinate with intelligent systems under conditions of customer presence, temporal pressure, and operational variability. Originality/value The paper introduces the symbioscape as a novel, three-tier environmental construct for human–machine collaboration, extending the servicescape from customer–employee encounters to hybrid human–AI work systems. It adds a missing environmental layer to human-machine collaboration research by systematically integrating dispersed insights on context into a coherent framework that links environmental cue structures to sensemaking and adaptation outcomes. For scholars, it offers an integrative conceptual architecture; for practitioners, it provides a foundation for designing and structuring future workplaces that foster adaptive human–machine collaboration.

items.title: The Happiness Backfire: Engagement-Oriented Brand Content Predicts Fewer Reposts and Shapes Comment Responses
items.abstract: Brand-owned social media increasingly carries messages about enjoyment, participation, connection, purpose, and achievement, yet the same message may not produce the same response. This study examines how engagement-oriented brand content relates to comments and reposts across two brand contexts. Using PERMA as a semantic coding standard, we analyze 1,191 official Weibo posts from McDonald’s and Burberry in 2025. A Python-assisted LLM pipeline provides pre-annotation, followed by two-researcher reviews. OLS and PPML show a robust negative association between engagement-oriented content and reposting, while the comment association is less stable. Brand-specific results show greater heterogeneity for reposting. We define this as a narrow happiness backfire: content built around active involvement can be less portable across users’ networks even when it invites direct response. The findings show that conversation and public diffusion are distinct communication goals, so content designed to invite participation should not be assumed to travel widely.

items.title: THE HISTORY AND FUTURE OF CHARACTER EDUCATION TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: This article examines the historical development of character education technologies, the pedagogical perspectives that have influenced their formation, and their potential for future advancement. It explores the traditions of folk pedagogy, the educational ideas of Eastern thinkers, and the distinctive characteristics of contemporary approaches to character education. Particular attention is given to the role of interactive methods, innovative pedagogical tools, and digital technologies in the educational process. The study emphasizes the importance of integrating national and universal human values, considering learners' individual characteristics, and developing independent thinking, social responsibility, and high moral standards. Furthermore, the article discusses the potential of artificial intelligence and modern technologies to enhance the effectiveness of character education in the future. items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Education: Perceptions of Undergraduate Medical Students in Northeastern Nigeria and Recommendations for Trainers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted in healthcare; however, the perceptions of undergraduate medical students in Nigeria on its role in clinical education remain underexplored. This study examined students’ perceptions of AI in clinical education across four public universities in Northeastern Nigeria. A mixed method cross-sectional survey was conducted between February and May, 2026 using a 27-items questionnaire. Convenience sampling approach was employed, and 200 valid responses were analysed. Likert data and free-text responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis, respectively. Overall, 85.5% of the respondents reported a basic understanding of AI, 49.5% reported familiarity with AI in healthcare and 38.5% reported regular exposure to AI tools during their training. Most of the students perceived potential educational benefits: 90% agreed that AI could improve the quality of learning, and 85.5% agreed that it could enhance clinical decision support. However, 86% expressed concern that overreliance on AI could negatively affect clinical reasoning and judgement, while 59.5% believed AI could reduce hands-on practical training, and 57% agreed that it could replace medical roles. Only 20.5% of the respondent agreed to have adequate AI training in their medical curricula, while 72.5% supported incorporating AI into their curriculum. These findings suggest that respondents generally held positive perceptions of AI on clinical education but perceived some concerns about its responsible use and preparation for AI-enabled healthcare.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED GAMIFIED TEACHING TECHNOLOGY IN 7TH-GRADE PHYSICS ON STUDENTS' ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT
items.abstract: In contemporary education, the integration of artificial intelligence and gamification elements has become an important direction for enhancing students’ learning motivation and improving the teaching of complex subjects such as physics. However, the impact of artificial intelligence-based gamified teaching technology on the academic achievement of 7th-grade physics students has not yet been sufficiently explored in practical terms. Therefore, the aim of this study was to determine the effect of artificial intelligence-based gamified teaching technology on students’ academic achievement in 7th-grade physics and to substantiate its effectiveness scientifically. The study employed theoretical analysis of scientific and methodological literature, questionnaires, pedagogical observation, and practical work through interactive tasks, while the collected data were processed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. The results showed positive relationships among students’ interest in physics, understanding of the topic, acceptance of game elements, and perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence support, and it was also found that EducaPlay-based tasks and AI-assisted guidance increased classroom engagement. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the practical description of the effect of integrating artificial intelligence and gamification elements in 7th-grade physics and in clarifying its pedagogical potential. In conclusion, artificial intelligence-based gamified teaching technology can be considered an effective pedagogical tool for increasing interest in physics, strengthening learning activity, and improving students’ mastery of educational content in 7th-grade physics.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF DIGITAL LITERACY ON DIGITAL ENTREPRENEURIAL INTENTION AMONG VIETNAMESE UNIVERSITY STUDENTS: THE SERIAL MEDIATING ROLES OF SELFEFFICACY AND PERCEIVED DESIRABILITY
items.abstract: This research project investigates how digital competencies influence Vietnamese university students' intentions to start digital businesses. Despite Vietnam's rapid digital transformation (73% internet penetration, $50 billion digital economy by 2025), only 4.7% of digitally active students pursue entrepreneurship. This study explains why. The study has three primary aims: 1 Test whether self-efficacy and perceived desirability serially mediate the relationship between digital literacy and digital entrepreneurial intention (DEI) 2 Examine whether family business background strengthens (moderates) this relationship 3 Identify multiple configurational pathways (equifinal configurations) leading to high DEI using fsQCA The research integrates the Entrepreneurial Event Model (EEM) and Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT) as its theoretical foundation. Methods Aspect Detail Design Quantitative, cross-sectional survey Sample 618 university students from 13 universities across Northern, Central, and Southern Vietnam Response rate 87.3% Sampling Stratified random (region, university type, discipline) Measures 7-point Likert scales (AI literacy, Fintech literacy, digital skills, self-efficacy, perceived desirability, DEI) Analysis PLS-SEM (5,000 bootstraps) + fsQCA (configurational) Expected Outcomes Direct Effects (H1-H5) All five direct paths are expected to be positive and significant (p < 0.001), with effect sizes ranging from β = 0.29 to 0.48. Serial Mediation (H6) The indirect path (DL → DSE → PD → DEI) is expected to be significant (indirect effect ≈ 0.074, p < 0.001), confirming that digital literacy works through psychological mechanisms rather than directly. Moderation (H7) Family business background is expected to positively moderate the DL–DEI relationship (β ≈ 0.19, p < 0.001), meaning students from entrepreneurial families benefit more from digital literacy. Configurational Pathways (H8) Three distinct pathways to high DEI are expected: Pathway Core conditions Technology-confident High digital literacy + High self-efficacy Passion-driven High perceived desirability + Family business background Balanced High levels of all three cognitive conditions Model Fit The model is expected to explain 54.8% of the variance in DEI (R² = 0.548), with SRMR = 0.062 and NFI = 0.912. Theoretical Contributions Extends EEM and SCCT as functionally sequential, not merely complementary Conceptualizes digital literacy as multidimensional (AI + Fintech + digital skills) Introduces family business background as a novel moderator Uses fsQCA to challenge net-effects logic Practical Contributions For universities: Integrated digital entrepreneurship curricula Experiential learning (hackathons, incubators) Differentiated student support based on configurational profiles For Vietnamese policymakers: "Digital Entrepreneurial Literacy" module (ChatGPT, Futurify, Canva/Shopify) "Student Digital Startup Hubs" at HUIT, Đà Nẵng University, Hà Nội University "Family-Backed Digital Entrepreneur" mentorship tracks Limitations Cross-sectional design (no causal inference; reverse causality possible) Self-report measures (social desirability bias) Single-country context (limited generalizability) Focus on intentions (not actual venture creation) Data Availability Upon acceptance, anonymized data, questionnaires (Vietnamese/English), SmartPLS model, fsQCA scripts, and ethics documents will be publicly available under CC-BY 4.0 license. items.title: The Impact of Time Pressure on Perceptions of Difficulty in an Automation-Supported Task
items.abstract: As automation progressively becomes integrated into decision-making environments, understanding why users fail to engage automated systems optimally remains crucial. The present study examined whether perceptions of time pressure could impact subjective and objective difficulty and its influence on use of discretionary automation. Seventy participants completed a visual search task under untimed and timed conditions, sometimes with the option to engage an automated aid. Results indicated that the time pressure increased both subjective and objective difficulty. Furthermore, participants used automation more frequently under the timed conditions. Despite the availability of a highly accurate system, participants did not engage the automation at rates to fully overcome the effects of time pressure. These findings suggest that users may turn to automation for support when task demands begin to increase, but these engagement decisions may not be driven to maximize performance outcomes.

items.title: The Importance of Physiotherapy in a Conservative Treatment of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
items.abstract: Purpose. The purpose of the study was to demonstrate the effect of selected physiotherapy methods in patients with a moderate form of carpal tunnel syndrome treated conservatively and to verify whether a one-month structured therapeutic programme leads to a measurable improvement in pain, joint mobility and swelling of the hand. Materials and Methods. An observational study was carried out in a group of 8 adult patients (4 women, 4 men) aged 39–71 years (mean age 56.25 years) with grade 2 carpal tunnel syndrome. Each patient underwent an entry examination comprising history taking, anthropometric measurement of upper-limb circumferences in the area of the forearm, wrist and metacarpal heads, goniometric measurement of the active and passive mobility of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb in the sagittal and frontal planes using the SFTR method, and pain assessment on a numeric rating scale. The therapeutic programme lasted one month and consisted of 8 sessions of 50 minutes; it included kinesiotherapy, manual therapy, proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation, stimulation of hand sensitivity, ultrasound applied to the palmar aspect of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb (3 MHz, 50 Hz, pulse-pause ratio 1:2, intensity 1.0–1.6 W·cm⁻²) and kinesiology taping. Input and output values were compared using the one-tailed paired t-test at a level of significance α = 0.05. Results. The range of motion of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb increased in both planes, for the active (sagittal plane p = 0.0001917; frontal plane p = 0.000005688) as well as for the passive range of motion (p = 0.00291 and p = 0.00002326). The intensity of pain decreased from a mean value of 4 to 2.625 (p = 0.00006782). The circumferences decreased in the area of the wrist (p = 0.01047) and of the metacarpal heads (p = 0.04749), while the forearm circumference remained unchanged. Conclusions. One month of targeted physiotherapy significantly reduced pain and swelling and improved the mobility of the thumb in patients with a moderate form of carpal tunnel syndrome. Conservative physiotherapeutic management combined with education in the principles of ergonomics can be recommended before considering surgical decompression in patients with a mild and moderate form of the syndrome.

items.title: The Influence of English Language Competence, Digital Literacy, Grit, and Technostress on Ship Crew Performance Mediated by Human Capital Capability
items.abstract: Crew performance determines the safety and operational efficiency of shipping companies, yet human factors remain the dominant cause of maritime accidents. This study aims to analyze the influence of English language competence, digital literacy, grit, and technostress on crew performance, with human capital capability serving as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed, utilizing a survey of 316 seafarers from shipping companies in Indonesia, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS. The results indicate that: 1) English language competence has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 2) Digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 3) Grit has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 4) Technostress does not have a significant effect on human capital capability; 5) English language competence does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 6) Digital literacy does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 7) Grit has a positive and significant effect on crew performance; 8) Technostress does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 9) Human capital capability has a positive and significant effect on crew performance; 10) Human capital capability fully mediates the effect of English language competence on crew performance; 11) Human capital capability fully mediates the effect of digital literacy on crew performance; 12) Human capital capability partially mediates the effect of grit on crew performance; 13) Human capital capability does not mediate the effect of technostress on crew performance. Shipping companies need to enhance crew performance by strengthening human capital capability through maritime English training, digital literacy development, and mental resilience building. The novelty of this study lies in examining human capital capability as a mediating mechanism among Indonesian seafarers.

items.title: The Invisible Work Behind an Innovation: Discarded Alternatives, Limits of Validity, and the Memory of Decisions / El trabajo invisible detrás de una innovación: alternativas descartadas, límites de validez y memoria de las decisiones
items.abstract: ENGLISH This critical essay examines the knowledge that may be lost when technological innovation is described only through its visible outcome. Drawing on work on invisible labour, articulation work, design rationale, knowledge boundaries and organizational learning, it distinguishes the context-dependent rejection of an alternative from evidence of its general infeasibility. The paper proposes a six-field record for preserving actual alternatives considered, criteria, gaps in evidence, responsible decisions and conditions for reconsideration. A hypothetical photopolymer case illustrates the difference between a selected option, an option rejected under defined constraints and an option left unresolved by insufficient evidence. The proposed record has not been empirically validated, does not claim methodological priority, and is explicitly distinguished from the author's earlier technical publications. Version 1. English and Spanish editions deposited together. items.title: The Mandate as a Unit of Risk — paper outline
items.abstract: This research outline sets out the proposed argument, derivations, evidence requirements and limitations for “The Mandate as a Unit of Risk.” The proposed paper connects the authority under which an AI agent acts with the economics of task reliability, oversight and adverse outcomes. It treats the mandate as a versioned authority for a class of acts, enforced through a permission that can be refused before an act is executed. The research programme examines how a mandate can express an admissible set of model-and-oversight configurations and a quantitative risk appetite, with authority narrowing automatically on independently adjudicated evidence and widening only with an authorised human signature. It extends the task-value framework with the cost of refusal and escalation, examines calibration in financial services, and identifies the conditions and limitations of any proposed assurance statement. The outline distinguishes established precedents from candidate contributions and identifies simulation and empirical work still required. Publication status: This deposit is a research outline, not a completed or peer-reviewed paper. Proposed theoretical results, calibration procedures and empirical tests remain to be established. Cordier’s simulation layer has not been independently rerun; the outline states the assumptions on which its proposed analysis depends.

items.title: The Mediating Role of Job Insecurity in the Relationship Between Technology Threat Perception and Organizational Commitment: An Investigation on Artificial Intelligence Anxiety
items.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of job insecurity in the relationships between technology threat perception, artificial intelligence anxiety, and organizational commitment. Data were collected from 387 full-time employees across multiple sectors in Türkiye through a cross-sectional survey. The hypothesized model was tested using structural equation modeling (AMOS 24), following confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrap-based mediation analysis (5,000 resamples). Technology threat perception and AI anxiety were both positively associated with job insecurity, which in turn was negatively associated with organizational commitment. Both stressors also showed significant direct negative associations with organizational commitment, and bootstrap analysis confirmed significant indirect effects through job insecurity, indicating complementary partial mediation. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is among the first studies to jointly model technology threat perception and AI anxiety as co-occurring antecedents of job insecurity within a single structural framework linking both to organizational commitment, extending cognitive stress appraisal theory, Conservation of Resources theory, and Social Exchange Theory to the context of AI-driven workplace change, with region-specific evidence from Türkiye.

items.title: The Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0: Integrating Imaging, Surgery, Transcatheter Therapies and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The management of mitral valve disease is rapidly evolving, driven by advances in multimodality imaging, surgical techniques, transcatheter therapies, and artificial intelligence (AI). In this changing landscape, the traditional Heart Team model should evolve toward a more integrated and dynamic multidisciplinary approach. The “Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0” may combine detailed anatomical and functional characterization with surgical expertise, transcatheter treatment options, and AI-assisted data integration to support individualized treatment strategies. Advanced imaging increasingly informs not only diagnosis but also procedural planning and patient selection, while AI may improve reproducibility of mitral regurgitation assessment, risk stratification, and phenotypic characterization. However, these technologies should augment rather than replace expert clinical judgment and shared decision-making. This Communication discusses the emerging components of this paradigm and proposes a practical framework in which imaging specialists, surgeons, interventional cardiologists, heart failure specialists, and data-driven tools interact throughout the patient pathway. The objective is not to create a larger Heart Team, but a more integrated one, capable of matching the right patient to the right treatment at the right time.

items.title: The Observer-Relative Interpretation Problem & The I or O Test™
items.abstract: The Observer-Relative Interpretation Problem & The I or O Test™ presents an evolving philosophical framework examining the relationship between observation, interpretation, identity, love, self-preservation, and continuity. The original working paper, developed October 23, 2026, investigates how different observers may encounter the same information yet arrive at different interpretations. It distinguishes physical and chemical information from meta-interpretation, proposing that the observer's perspective influences understanding without necessarily changing the underlying reality. An experimental appendix, developed October 28, 2026, introduces The I or O Test™, a proposed six-photograph observation exercise followed by personal explanation, a provisional trial period, and consideration of traceable behavioral evidence. The experiment introduces three observer-relative outcomes: I: Passed with insufficient evidence. O: Failed the experiment's stated criteria. i: The observed individual provided an explanation that convinced the observer. The appendix further develops the Birth Star Principle™, proposing that individuals differ in what they regard as essential to their self-preservation. Additional symbolic concepts include Pearly's Continuation, the collaboration of O and I through love, and the emergence of Newi. The central philosophical proposition is that observation does not confer complete knowledge of another individual. Interpretation remains provisional, and the observer must remain willing to correct their own understanding. This publication is an original, exploratory philosophical proposal. Its symbolic terminology and experimental classifications are not scientifically validated psychological assessments, diagnostic categories, or established physical laws. items.title: The Path of a Young Researcher: A Practical Guide for Students of the Presidential Academy
items.abstract: This practical guide, prepared by the Student Scientific Society of the Presidential Academy (RANEPA), supports students taking their first steps in research. It is structured as a journey map of eight stages: understanding science, finding sources, conducting research, writing, publishing, presenting, growing and getting support, and being part of the academic community. The guide explains how scientific knowledge differs from opinion, how academic degrees, titles and positions are organized, and how science is governed and funded in Russia. It covers systematic literature search, including eLIBRARY, CyberLeninka and the RANEPA library. It also covers research design (problem, object, subject, aim, objectives, hypothesis and methods) and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in line with the Academy’s Academic Integrity and AI Policy. Further sections address academic writing and the IMRAD structure, citation styles, plagiarism and originality, and choosing journals indexed in RSCI or listed by the Higher Attestation Commission and the Unified State List of Scientific Journals. They also explain how to recognize predatory publications, the peer-review process, and preparing conference presentations. Finally, the guide describes scholarships, grants, the student research portfolio and the structure of the Student Scientific Society. Each section includes step-by-step instructions, screenshots, QR codes to official resources and practical tips. A glossary of key terms is included. Keywords: young researcher, student research, academic writing, research design, scientific publishing, academic integrity, student scientific society, RANEPA

items.title: The Potential of AI-Powered Reflective Tools in Teacher Education
items.abstract: This chapter explores how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is influencing reflective practice in second language teacher education, along with the discussion on ethics and the developmental implications of AI-powered reflection. It conceptualizes AI-powered reflection as a form of technological mediation that alters how teaching experience is externalized and interpreted through algorithmic processes. Grounding in distributed cognition, this chapter positions AI as a cognitive artifact that shapes reflective activity while teacher professional meaning-making and accountability remains situated in teachers’ judgment. It shows how the influence of algorithmic mediation on reflective authority, agency and temporal depth has specific implications for professional novice teachers. Ethical considerations are presented as fundamental to the responsible integration of AI-powered reflective tools. The chapter further introduces a human-centered framework to inform their design and pedagogical use in teacher education and identifies future directions for research and practice that seek to sustain reflective depth and teacher agency within mentoring relationships and professional learning contexts. It concludes that AI can enhance reflective support when its use is guided by ethical commitments and remains aligned with the developmental purposes of professional development.

items.title: The Prestige: Benchmarking Cognitive Visual Reasoning using Magic Tricks
items.abstract: We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.

items.title: The Relationship Between Breakfast Habits and Work Productivity Among Production Department Workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia in 2026
items.abstract: Work productivity reflects the extent to which workers are able to carry out their responsibilities effectively during the production process. Workers’ eating patterns, including whether they consume breakfast before starting their activities, may be relevant to their physical readiness and ability to perform their tasks. This study examined the association between breakfast habits and work productivity among production department workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia in 2026. A quantitative observational study using a cross-sectional design was carried out among 120 production department workers, from whom 55 respondents were included as the study sample. Information regarding breakfast habits and work productivity was obtained through questionnaires. The collected data were subsequently analyzed using the Chi-Square test with Continuity Correction. Among the 55 respondents, 40 workers (72.7%) reported that they did not have a regular breakfast habit, whereas 15 workers (27.3%) reported having a breakfast habit. Regarding productivity, 37 respondents (67.3%) were categorized as having low work productivity, while 18 respondents (32.7%) were categorized as having high productivity. Statistical analysis produced a p-value of 0.003 (p < 0.05), demonstrating a significant association between breakfast habits and work productivity. The proportion of workers with high productivity was greater among those who reported having breakfast than among those who did not. The study concludes that breakfast habits are significantly associated with work productivity among production department workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia. items.title: The relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity - the mediating role of managerial culture
items.abstract: Purpose Knowledge work is extensively location-independent, making flexible work designs more common. However, organizations foster various practices regarding the level of autonomy and control, affecting employee well-being and productivity. To support strategic and operative work design, this paper aims to explain the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity, considering the mediating role of managerial culture. Design/methodology/approach This paper describes a quantitative survey featuring 1,057 respondents. It tests with a regression analysis a hypothesized model, in which the level of individual work autonomy, mediated by managerial culture, predicts well-being and productivity. Findings The analysis indicated that decision-making autonomy has a direct positive relationship with productivity. Furthermore, autonomy in working practices has a direct positive relationship with both well-being and productivity. Managerial culture mediates the relationship between decision-making autonomy and both outcome variables. Originality/value This paper provides empirical evidence of the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity. The academic value of this paper lies in the multiple dimensions of autonomy it addresses, yielding novel data on the outcomes in a comparative manner. As a pragmatic contribution, it provides input to managerial culture design.

items.title: The Relationships Between Artificial Intelligence-Induced Job Insecurity, Affective Commitment, Job Performance and Turnover Intention
items.abstract: This study examines the relationships between artificial intelligence-induced job insecurity, affective commitment, job performance, and turnover intention, with particular attention to the mediating roles of affective commitment and job performance. The analyses were conducted using structural equation modeling to assess the direct and indirect relationships among the variables. Data were collected from 400 employees working in different sectors through online and face-to-face surveys using a convenience sampling method. The findings indicate that AI-induced job insecurity is positively associated with turnover intention and negatively associated with affective commitment, whereas its direct association with job performance is not statistically significant. Affective commitment is positively associated with job performance and negatively associated with turnover intention. The mediation analyses indicate that affective commitment significantly mediates the relationships between AI-induced job insecurity and turnover intention and between AI-induced job insecurity and job performance. In contrast, the mediating role of job performance in the relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and turnover intention is not supported. Overall, the findings suggest that affective commitment represents an important explanatory pathway in the relationships between AI-induced job insecurity and employees’ work-related outcomes.

items.title: The Role of AI in Dementia Caregiving - A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Background: Dementia is a growing public health issue, one that burdens many, with a heavy reliance on familial relationships for support and care. This is an especially pressing issue within ethnically diverse (ED) communities. In parallel, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is also a rapidly growing industry, with many of its aspects being used in healthcare and patient management. Healthcare and AI have a reciprocal relationship. Today, AI can assist with many aspects of healthcare, such as assisting dementia caregivers through providing additional support. While this is a strong approach, before widespread use, it is important to be aware of its benefits, harms and ethical implications, since there is limited knowledge available on the topic and uninformed use can be detrimental. Aims and objectives: The aim of this study is to understand how AI can be used within the role of dementia caregiving. The objective is to understand AI uses’ barriers, enablers and the ethical issues that are prevalent, specifically for ED communities, dissecting if AI use for such sensitive topics would be appropriate or even feasible. Methods: For this scoping review various databases would be searched for articles on AI use in dementia caregiving and then screened in Covidence for relevance before data analysis. Grey literature would also be screened and reviewed. Significance: Dementia is a public health priority, it burdens many, especially within ED communities making it important to identify tools to assist with caregiving. This study would give an insight into how AI could be appropriately involved in dementia caregiving without imposing ethically.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Mediating the Influence of Language Literacy on the Academic Writing Skills of Politeknik Negeri Ambon Students
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the influence of Language Literacy on Academic Writing Ability with Artificial Intelligence as a mediating variable in Ambon State Polytechnic students. Academic writing ability is one of the important competencies that students must have in producing quality scientific work. However, the development of Artificial Intelligence technology has changed the learning patterns and academic writing processes of students. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method. The study population was Ambon State Polytechnic students, with a sample of 50 respondents determined using a purposive sampling technique. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) based on Partial Least Square (PLS) with the help of SmartPLS 4. The results of the study indicate that Language Literacy has a positive and significant effect on Artificial Intelligence, Artificial Intelligence has a positive and significant effect on Academic Writing Ability, while Language Literacy has a positive but insignificant effect on Academic Writing Ability. In addition, Artificial Intelligence is proven to significantly mediate the relationship between Language Literacy and Academic Writing Ability. The results of the study indicate that Artificial Intelligence acts as a full mediator in this relationship. This finding indicates that the improvement of students' academic writing ability is not only determined by language literacy skills, but also by the ability to utilize Artificial Intelligence effectively in the learning process and academic writing.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Development of Creativity Skills According to Teachers and Students
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has renewed debates on the nature of creativity. This study examines the role of artificial intelligence in the development of creativity skills among middle school teachers and students through comparative perspectives. Using a qualitative case study design, the research involved 87 participants—42 teachers from different subject areas and 45 eighth-grade students—from public middle schools in Bursa, Turkey, during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed via content analysis. The findings reveal that AI plays a dual role in the creative process: it facilitates idea generation and imagination, yet may restrict originality when used without pedagogical guidance. While students tend to view artificial intelligence as a tool that accelerates production, teachers emphasize risks such as cognitive offloading and superficial learning. Artificial intelligence becomes an effective educational tool only when embedded within ethically grounded, teacher-guided, and AI literacy–oriented frameworks. Subject-based analyses show that, particularly in Science and Mathematics, teachers position AI as a supportive cognitive partner that facilitates visualization and conceptual understanding, yet caution that unguided use may replace deep learning with surface-level content production.

items.title: The Smart School Model: Integrating Intelligent Agents and IoT for Autonomous, Ethical and Reproducible Educational Management
items.abstract: Smart-school projects increasingly combine sensors, dashboards and artificial intelligence, but their managerial value remains weak when attendance, access control, energy use and reporting operate as isolated modules. This paper proposes a Smart School Management System (SSMS) in which Internet-of-Things observations are transformed into auditable decisions through a policy-constrained multi-agent architecture. Unlike component-level smart-campus prototypes, the contribution is an orchestration model linking perception agents, decision agents and a coordination agent under privacy, traceability and human-oversight constraints. The empirical part uses the open UCI Occupancy Detection dataset (20,560 labelled records) to validate the perception layer on a reproducible occupancy-classification task. Trained on 8,143 records and tested on 12,417 records, logistic regression achieved 98.34% accuracy and 0.9659 F1-score, outperforming a simple light-threshold rule (94.36% accuracy, 0.8961 F1). These results validate only the occupancy-perception component under the stated open-data protocol; they do not validate the complete smart-school system or institutional deployment. The paper therefore advances a reproducible, ethically governed and practically deployable direction for autonomous educational management.

items.title: The Study of Digital Transformation, Artificial Intelligence and Their Implications for Future Research
items.abstract: Digital transformation changes the conditions under which organizations produce and use knowledge. Artificial intelligence adds new ways to search, predict, generate, and evaluate information. Yet greater use of these tools does not establish that research becomes more reliable or more original. This paper develops a critical narrative review and descriptive secondary-data analysis to examine that distinction. Selected publications on organizational change, AI-assisted work, scientific discovery, and governance provide the conceptual foundation. Published statistics from Stanford's AI Index and Eurostat illustrate changes in adoption between 2023 and 2025. The two series are analysed separately because their populations and measurement procedures differ. The evidence indicates expanding use, but adoption statistics cannot demonstrate causal improvements in research quality. An original conceptual framework links digital foundations and AI capabilities with changes in research practice, conditioned by human expertise, institutional arrangements, and governance. Four propositions translate the framework into questions for future testing. The proposed agenda prioritizes reproducibility, task-specific evaluation, skill development, equitable participation, and preservation of intellectual diversity. The paper concludes that future research should evaluate the complete knowledge-production process, including verification and correction costs, rather than treating faster output as sufficient evidence of progress. No primary survey, experiment, or model validation is claimed. The contribution is an integrated account of how organizations can study AI-enabled transformation while maintaining the evidentiary standards needed for credible knowledge

items.title: The Usability of Ranked Choice Voting in Digital Ballot Formats
items.abstract: ObjectiveThree digital ranked choice voting ballots were investigated to assess the impact of formatting on usability.BackgroundRanked choice voting (RCV) is a ballot format that allows voters to rank candidate choices in order of preference. The design of the ballot has a notable impact on usability, and this remains a challenge for RCV.MethodThis experiment investigated the usability of three RCV electronic ballot formats (bubble grid, column, and hand-numbered). Completion times, errors, subjective usability ratings, and trust data were collected.ResultsThe three formats took subjects 50-70 seconds on average to vote for a single contest. The ballots also had high error rates, which ranged from 23-38%. The hand-numbered format had the worst performance, as it had the highest completion times, error rates, and the lowest subjective usability ratings.ConclusionThis research highlights usability issues with RCV digital ballots. The formats tested were inefficient and ineffective, and performed poorly in comparison to previously tested plurality digital ballots.ApplicationThis experiment raises concerns about the scalability of RCV to larger elections. Ballots with RCV take longer to vote on and have higher error rates, which should be taken into consideration by election administrators.

items.title: The Use of Generative AI in Second Language Writing: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping second language (L2) writing by introducing new forms of interaction between learners and intelligent technologies. This conceptual paper examines the potential opportunities and critical challenges of GenAI in L2 writing, drawing on a purposively selected body of recent scholarship. It suggests that GenAI can provide contingent support throughout the writing process, facilitate idea generation and revision, and expand opportunities for multilingual composing through L1-mediated and translanguaging practices. At the same time, excessive reliance on AI may lead to cognitive offloading and weaken learners’ engagement in higher-order writing processes. Concerns about inaccurate information and fabricated citations further highlight the need for independent verification and critical AI literacy. Moreover, unequal access to technological resources, AI literacy, and educational support may contribute to an emerging AI divide and reproduce existing educational and linguistic inequalities. The paper argues that the pedagogical value of GenAI depends on how it is integrated into learners’ writing processes and on whether it supports sustained engagement, learner agency, and reflective thinking and decision-making without displacing their intellectual and authorial responsibilities.

items.title: Topological Multi-Connectivity of Distributed Cognitive Systems: Pairwise-Contact “Foams”, Individuality Without Dissolution, and a Falsiable Research Program
items.abstract: Can an agent be in contact with all other agents without being dissolved in them? We give this question a precise topological form. A pairwise-contact foam is a family of regions ("bubbles") of a state space with pairwise disjoint interiors, which represent the preserved individuality of each agent, such that every two regions touch, which represents connection, ideally along a set of positive size. We show that the naive formulation of the condition is degenerate unless the regions are regular closed with nonempty interior, and that point contact is cheap in dimension \( \ge2 \) while contact along arcs is impossible in the plane for more than four disks. We then prove that foams exist for every number \( N\ge2 \) of regions and, in the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \( \ell^2 \), for countably infinitely many regions covering the whole space: the regions \( D_k=\{x:|x_k|\ge|x_j|\ \forall j\} \) meet pairwise along codimension-one walls \( x_k=\pm x_l \). In dimension three and on orientable surfaces of higher genus the planar obstruction is bypassed as well. Gluing along contact sets leaves every piece intact, which is the formal sense of "union without dissolution". Pairwise contact is strictly weaker than the Wada property, and riddled basins are a degenerate, non-proper case. For empirical use we separate three quantities that are easily confused: the global separation \( d(C_i,C_j) \) of two regions, the switching distance \( d(x,C_j) \) from a given state, and the activation distance to the contact set, together with intervention-specific versions that depend on an actuation model. We replace a single adjacency density by the spectrum of separations, a threshold-free completion scale, and a persistent nerve, with explicit limits on what the nerve proves, dimension-aware null models, and a rule that unsupported regions make a test inconclusive rather than being deleted. No empirical result is claimed. The interpretive layer (cognitive light cone, "noosphere") is kept strictly apart from the mathematical and testable layers.

items.title: Towards a Cognitive Behavioural Occupational Health Practice
items.abstract: This chapter outlines the personal and professional foundations of the cognitive behavioural approach developed for occupational health practice. Both occupational health and cognitive behavioural therapy became a vocation for me, providing a stabilising and meaningful thread that supported my movement beyond personal adversity and shaped my progression from nursing into trauma therapy and expert-witness work. The chapter traces a 40-year professional journey alongside the evolution of occupational health, from its earlier focus on industrial injury to its current role as a clinically grounded specialty. It considers how changes in the nature of work, together with increasing recognition of psychological and social influences on health, have reshaped contemporary occupational health practice. My thinking has been strongly influenced by the work of Gordon Waddell, Tom Cox, Cary Cooper and others whose research laid the foundations for biopsychosocial and psychologically informed approaches to work and health. These influences supported my development as both an occupational health practitioner and cognitive behavioural therapist and continue to guide my clinical reasoning. This chapter therefore introduces the values, evidence base and reasoning that underpin the cognitive behavioural approach explored throughout this book.

items.title: Towards Task-Oriented Semantic Communication: A Survey on Technologies, Opportunities, and Challenges
items.abstract: The growing demand for intelligent and adaptive services is accelerating the transition from conventional communication systems to semantic communication. Task-Oriented Semantic Communication (ToSC) has emerged as an efficient framework that reduces communication cost by transmitting only task-relevant information for downstream processing. This survey reviews the theoretical foundations, system architectures, and enabling technologies of ToSC, providing a taxonomy of design strategies spanning collaborative edge inference, end-to-end optimization, and multi-agent cooperation. Key technologies, including deep learning-based semantic representation and adaptive joint source-channel coding, are discussed. Device heterogeneity and partial observability are examined alongside recent tasks' performance evaluations, such as classification and recognition. The survey also discusses the integration of large-scale multimodal foundation models into semantic encoders for zero-shot task adaptation, continual learning frameworks for on-device semantic processing, cooperative multi-agent reasoning with interpretable information exchange, and cross-layer co-design within AI-native 6G infrastructures, leveraging reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and digital twins. By consolidating existing knowledge and identifying key design trade-offs in latency, accuracy, and bandwidth efficiency, this work aims to serve as both a reference and a roadmap for advancing ToSC toward reliable and resource-efficient communication in 6G and beyond.
